idiom_name: immutable identity member + explicit key-generation strategy + mapper read-back
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the entity one immutable identity member whose type is the storage key, and treat its unsaved state (absent/null) as a mapping concern rather than a domain rule. Choose the key generator deliberately: database identity or sequence columns (read the value back after the INSERT), a key table handing out ranges (hi-lo) when compact keys must be known before the insert, or an application-side UUID/ULID/snowflake generator when the key must exist before the row. The mapper has three duties - copy the key out of the row on load, write a generated key back onto the object after insert, and target update/delete by key rather than by business fields - and every consumer that needs identity (identity map, unit of work, foreign-key mapping, caches, audit logs) is fed that same key. Never recompute or mutate it.
code_sketch:
class Order:
    id: Key | None = None          # identity member, immutable once set

# load
order = Order(); order.id = row["id"]
# insert with a database-generated key
order.id = db.execute("INSERT INTO orders (...) VALUES (...) RETURNING id", params).scalar()
# update / delete always target the key
db.execute("UPDATE orders SET ... WHERE id = :id", {"id": order.id})
pitfalls: An entity whose generated key is never written back cannot be updated or cached afterwards - it looks new on every save.
Using mutable business fields as identity breaks identity maps, caches and foreign keys as soon as that data is corrected.
Sharing one key-generation sequence across unrelated tables couples their write paths and makes key ranges ambiguous.
Treating 0 or the empty string as 'no key yet' leaks a persistence convention into the domain model.

Putting an entity into a HashSet or HashMap before it is persisted (id is null), then calling persist which sets the id and silently changes the hashCode — the object becomes unfindable in its own collection. Fix: only add to sets/maps after first persist, or return a stable placeholder hashCode before persistence.
Treating equals and hashCode as based on business fields while the ORM uses the identity field — the two views diverge and the identity map silently returns the wrong instance.
Using a sequential integer key in a public API or URL: an attacker can enumerate all resource IDs with a simple script. Always substitute a UUID, ULID or opaque token for external exposure.

Failing to handle OptimisticLockException (or equivalent) when a concurrent transaction has updated the same row — a stale entity is silently overwritten unless the version number check aborts the write.

Clock skew or monotonic-counter drift with time-based UUIDs (v7, ULID) causing duplicate IDs when two nodes generate IDs in the same millisecond without coordination; mitigations include node-specific bits (Snowflake) or a central sequence.
Composite primary keys requiring a separate identifier class whose equals/hashCode must be implemented correctly; many ORM bugs stem from comparing composite keys by reference instead of by value.

Renumbering keys during data migration or database consolidation while URL bookmarks, cache entries, foreign-key columns and identity-map entries still hold the old values — the result is orphaned or misrouted references.

Exposing the internal surrogate key alongside a business key in an API with no rule about which one is authoritative — clients that cache one and servers that resolve the other disagree about identity.

Wrong move: assume a database-generated IDENTITY key exists before INSERT -> Y fails: a child graph, idempotency key or batch record cannot refer to the object yet -> instead Z: generate UUID/ULID/sequence values before INSERT when pre-insert identity is required, or use INSERT ... RETURNING and propagate the returned key.

Wrong move: treat a sequential primary key as an authorization boundary -> Y fails: an attacker can enumerate neighboring IDs or exploit IDOR even when the object exists -> instead Z: authorize every object lookup and use a non-guessable external token or UUID as defense in depth.

Wrong move: expose a tenant-local integer as globally unique -> Y fails: the same ID can resolve to another tenant when a lookup omits tenant scope -> instead Z: carry tenant_id through key, foreign keys, identity-map/cache keys and authorization predicates.
